questions.explanation:
Hint: Conjugated double bond system is more stable. Explanation: This reaction involves treating an \(\alpha\)-hydroxy ester with concentrated \(\text{HBr}\), which is a strong acid and a source of \(\text{Br}^-\). Protonation of the \(\text{OH}\) group: The hydroxyl \(\text{OH}\) group is a poor leaving group. In the presence of concentrated \(\text{HBr}\), it gets protonated to form a better leaving group, a protonated alcohol ( \(\text{-OH}_2^+\)). The starting material is \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{C}(=\text{CH}_2)\text{COOCH}_3\). The \(\text{OH}\) group is on the carbon adjacent to the\(\text{C}=\text{C}\)double bond. Loss of water and carbocation formation: The \(\text{-OH}_2^+\) group departs as a neutral \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) molecule, forming a secondary carbocation at the \(\alpha\)-carbon (the carbon that previously held the \(\text{OH}\) group). The resulting carbocation is \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{C}(=\text{CH}_2)\text{COOCH}_3\). Carbocation rearrangement (Allylic rearrangement): The initially formed secondary carbocation is adjacent to a \(\text{C}=\text{C}\) double bond. This allows for resonance stabilization and an allylic rearrangement where the positive charge shifts to the \(\gamma-\)carbon (the terminal \(\text{CH}_2\) of the original double bond). The rearranged, and more stable, allylic carbocation is \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{COOCH}_3)\text{CH}_2^+\). Nucleophilic attack: The bromide ion \(\text{Br}^-\) acts as a nucleophile and attacks the more stable primary carbocation (\(\text{CH}_2^+\)). This results in the major product \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{COOCH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\).
